Led by principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators such as David Keith, the initiative was publicly discussed, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. Importantly, SCoPEx was not designed to cool the planet or test geoengineering deployment; rather, it sought to enhance computer models assessing the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering strategies. The experiment involved a scientific balloon gondola operating at around 20 km altitude, releasing a minimal quantity of material—typically calcium carbonate—around 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms, into a defined volume. Subsequent measurements would focus on aerosol microphysics and light scattering. A planned test in Sweden in 2021 was limited to hardware evaluation and was ultimately canceled pending societal engagement, with no aerosol particles released. In March 2024, Harvard announced that the SCoPEx initiative was no longer being pursued, and the platform will now be redirected for unrelated stratospheric research, highlighting the need for careful consideration of ecological impacts and community concerns.

A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released.
